title: Multilevel Amortized Gaussian Elimination in Information-Set Decoding: Applications to HQC and PCG
authors: Kévin Carrier, Valérian Hatey, Laura Luzzi, and Jean-Pierre Tillich
abstract:
For cryptosystems whose security relies on the hardness of decoding in the sublinear regime, the best known attacks are based on Information Set Decoding (ISD). In this regime, which is particularly relevant to HQC and Pseudorandom Correlation Generators (PCG), the cost of Gaussian elimination is no longer negligible and significantly affects the overall attack complexity.

In this work, we revisit the Reduce-and-Prange technique of Kim and Lee, which reduces the cost of Gaussian elimination by reusing partial pivots. We refine its complexity analysis using branching-process techniques, thereby obtaining a more accurate assessment of its performance. We then extend partial pivot reuse to Stern's algorithm and introduce MAGE-Stern, a multilevel amortized Gaussian elimination variant of Stern's algorithm.

Under a consistent logic-gate cost model, MAGE-Stern improves upon the best previously known attack against HQC by approximately 3 bits in time complexity, while reducing the memory complexity by about 12 bits. In particular, we estimate the security of the standardized HQC Category I parameter set at approximately 140 bits, about 3 bits below its NIST security target. We further combine multilevel amortized Gaussian elimination with the projective decoding framework of Carrier, Hatey, and Tillich, and investigate its application to regular decoding. Applied to the reference Pseudorandom Correlation Generator (PCG) parameter sets of Boyle, Couteau, Gilboa, and Ishai, the resulting algorithms improve upon the best previously known attacks by up to 6 bits across a broad range of practical parameters.

1     Introduction
1.1    Decoding in the Sublinear Regime and the HQC Cryptosystem
A large class of code-based cryptosystems derives its security from the hardness
of the decoding problem.

and e ∈ Fnq of Hamming weight t. The goal is to recover the error vector e.

    This is notably the case for the HQC cryptosystem [2], which was recently
selected by NIST for standardization. More precisely, the security of HQC re-
lies on the hardness of a variant of the decoding problem over F2 , namely the
Decoding-One-Out-of-Many (DOOM) problem, in which an attacker is given k

regime, where k = Rn, R ∈ [0, 1] and t = Θ( n) = o(n).

logarithmic cost for Stern, but a unit cost for Progressive Sieving-ISD. Second,

    As discussed above, the results of [22] suggest that, for HQC, further improve-
ments are more likely to come from reducing the polynomial factors than from
refining the asymptotic exponent. In this context, reducing the cost of Gaussian
elimination becomes especially important, as linear algebra constitutes one of
the dominant costs of an ISD iteration. A first approach, proposed by Canteaut
and Chabaud [13], and later refined by Bernstein, Lange and Peters [7], updates
the information set by exchanging only one coordinate between consecutive it-
erations. This reduces the cost of Gaussian elimination from cubic to quadratic
but introduces strong dependencies between successive iterations, which offset
the expected linear speedup in the sublinear regime.
    More recently, Kim and Lee [30] introduced a different strategy for Prange’s
algorithm [36], called Reduce-and-Prange (RaP). Instead of recomputing a full
Gaussian elimination at each iteration, their algorithm progressively constructs
the information set through a sequence of partial reductions, each requiring
a smaller Gaussian elimination. Each partial reduction is repeated sufficiently
many times to validate the corresponding partial guess. The resulting tree struc-
ture provides a much finer control over the dependencies introduced by these
partial reductions and leads to the best known practical Gaussian elimination
reduction for Prange’s algorithm.
    Beyond HQC, reducing the cost of linear algebra is also of practical inter-
est for decoding over large finite fields, where Gaussian elimination remains a
dominant component of the overall complexity.


1.2   Decoding over Large Fields and the Security of PCG Protocols

The security of many Pseudorandom Correlation Generator (PCG) protocols
relies on the hardness of the decoding problem or its regular counterpart over
large finite fields [39,44,27,4,20,19,38,12,37]. In particular, [10] proposed refer-
ence parameter sets over the field F2128 , which are widely used to evaluate the
security of PCG constructions.
    The large-field setting fundamentally changes the behavior of Information Set
Decoding algorithms. Indeed, an ISD algorithm enumerating vectors of weight
p incurs an enumeration cost containing the factor (q − 1)p . When q is large,
this factor rapidly dominates the overall complexity, making the enumeration of
vectors of positive weight prohibitively expensive.
    As a consequence, it was shown in [14] that, as q → +∞, all known ISD al-
gorithms become asymptotically equivalent to Prange’s algorithm. Accordingly,
the security of current PCG parameter sets is primarily evaluated using Prange’s
4                               K. Carrier, V. Hatey, L. Luzzi, J-P. Tillich

algorithm and its practical improvements, such as the Reduce-and-Prange algo-
rithm of [30]. In the regular setting, these attacks also compete with algebraic
and hybrid attacks [11,42,30].
    Recently, [18] showed that ISD algorithms can be adapted to the projec-
tive space. By enumerating projective equivalence classes rather than vectors
themselves, one factor of (q − 1) is removed from the enumeration cost. Conse-
quently, projective ISD algorithms can consider non-zero enumeration weights
while avoiding the prohibitive penalty associated with large fields.
    This observation calls into question the current security evaluation of PCG
protocols and suggests that projective ISD algorithms should also be taken into
account when calibrating their parameters.

1.3   Our Contributions
We first revisit the theoretical analysis of the Reduce-and-Prange algorithm
of [30]. Its success probability was previously estimated as a product of inde-
pendent events. We show that these events are in fact correlated and that the
evolution of the algorithm is more accurately described by the survival of a
multitype branching process. This yields a corrected expression for the success
probability and shows that the analysis of [30] overestimates it. We also refine
the algorithm by allowing the number of repetitions to vary across reduction
levels. The resulting parameters govern a tradeoff between the cost of each ex-
ecution and the survival probability of the branching process, and their joint
optimization leads to a lower overall complexity.

    Building on this analysis, we introduce Multilevel Amortized Gaussian Elim-
ination for Stern’s algorithm (MAGE-Stern), which incorporates the multilevel
Gaussian-elimination technique of [30] into Stern’s algorithm. We analyze its
success probability through the same branching-process framework and apply it
to the security evaluation of HQC under a theoretical cost model aligned with
the NIST security requirements. In this model, Gaussian elimination accounts
for a substantial fraction of the computational cost, making its amortization
particularly effective. Compared with classical Stern, MAGE-Stern reduces the
attack complexity by approximately 3 bits and the memory complexity by ap-
proximately 12 bits. The reduction in Gaussian-elimination cost also shifts the
optimal enumeration weight from p = 5 to p = 3, thereby reducing both the
running-time and memory contributions associated with list enumeration from
cubic to quadratic in n. Applied to the official HQC parameter sets, MAGE-
Stern yields the security estimates reported in Tables 6.3 and 6.4, making it the
most efficient known attack against HQC. In particular, our analysis estimates
the security of the current HQC Category I parameters at approximately 140
bits, about 3 bits below the NIST target of 143 bits.

    Extending our approach to the non-binary setting over large finite fields, we
introduce Projective-MAGE-Stern by combining the projective decoding frame-
work of [18] with multilevel amortized Gaussian elimination. We then extend this

approach to decoding problems with regular error structure by incorporating the
partial-guessing strategy of [25,30], resulting in Regular-Projective-MAGE-Stern.
For the large-field parameter sets proposed in [10], using projective representa-
tions in the meet-in-the-middle step of ISD allows vectors of weight p = 2 to be
enumerated without paying the usual factor of (q − 1). Projective-MAGE-Stern
therefore combines the increased success probability of Projective-Stern with
the reduced Gaussian elimination cost of Reduce-and-Prange. Its application,
together with that of its regular counterpart, to the reference PCG parame-

Projective-MAGE-Stern improves upon Reduce-and-Prange by up to 10 bits
and upon the attacks selected by the estimator of [46] by up to 6 bits. Overall,
Projective-MAGE-Stern and Regular-Projective-MAGE-Stern provide the best
known attacks for a broad range of the PCG parameter sets proposed in [10].

2.3   Branching Processes in a Varying Environment
The Reduce-and-Prange algorithm [30], which will be discussed later, improves
upon Prange’s algorithm by factoring parts of the Gaussian elimination step.
Roughly speaking, it proceeds recursively by making partial Prange bets: at a
given level, the algorithm tries several small sets of positions and bets that the
error vector vanishes on these positions. Whenever such a bet is correct, the
original decoding problem can be reduced to a smaller decoding problem, to
which the same strategy is then applied recursively.
    The analysis of this recursive structure can be refined beyond the treatment
of [30] by using classical probabilistic tools. Indeed, the algorithm naturally
gives rise to a tree of partial bets: successful bets generate new subproblems,
whereas unsuccessful branches die out. Such a structure is naturally modeled by
a branching process; see, for instance, the classical references [29,3]. Moreover,
since the distribution governing the number of surviving branches may vary from
one reduction level to the next, the appropriate framework is that of branching
processes in varying environments.

2.4     Multinomial Distribution

The offspring distributions considered in our branching processes will be bino-
mial distributions. This will allow us to analyze the Reduce-and-Prange algo-
rithm and our variant. However, in Section 5, we will also generalize this ap-
proach to Stern’s algorithm. In that setting, we will use multitype branching

This section surveys the best-known combinatorial attacks against HQC and
PCG. The techniques presented here are well established in the literature. How-
ever, they have not been considered together in the context of HQC and PCG,
nor analyzed in the computational models that are most relevant for our security

3.2   The Reduce-and-Prange Algorithm.

Stern’s algorithm improves upon Prange’s algorithm by using a birthday-paradox
strategy to relax the condition imposed on the error vector inside the informa-
tion set. Another natural way to improve upon Prange is to keep the same bet,
namely eI = 0, while reducing the cost of each iteration. Since a Prange itera-
tion is dominated by Gaussian elimination, whose cost is only polynomial, such
an improvement does not change the exponential complexity. However, in the
regime considered here, where t = o(n), linear-algebra costs are no longer neg-
ligible and reducing them can lead to significant practical speedups. The main
difficulty is then to amortize Gaussian elimination without introducing excessive
dependencies between successive trials.
    A method introduced by Canteaut and Chabaud [13], and later refined by
Bernstein, Lange and Peters [7], proposed such an improvement based on local
updates of the information set. Starting from an initial information set I, each
iteration replaces c columns of I with c columns outside I, chosen uniformly at
random, while preserving the information-set property. The Gaussian elimination
is then updated from the previous one rather than recomputed from scratch.
    This procedure induces a random walk on the set of information sets. Its
main benefit is to substantially reduce the linear-algebra cost per iteration. Its
drawback is that consecutive information sets differ only slightly and are there-
fore strongly correlated. As a consequence, the corresponding success events are
no longer independent, and more iterations may be required than in the ideal-
ized independent setting. The overall complexity is thus governed by a trade-off
between cheaper iterations and a potentially larger number of trials.

5     Adapting Reduce-and-Prange to Stern’s Algorithm
In this section, we extend the Reduce-and-Prange framework to Stern’s ISD
algorithm and to the DOOM setting. The purpose of this extension is to amor-
tize the cost of Gaussian elimination across several iterations. Consequently, the
approach is beneficial only when Gaussian elimination constitutes a significant
fraction of the cost of an iteration.
    This condition is automatically satisfied for Prange’s algorithm, since each
iteration essentially consists of performing Gaussian elimination. Stern’s algo-
rithm, however, additionally involves a meet-in-the-middle step. In the linear-
weight regime, where t grows linearly with n, this step dominates the cost of
an iteration, leaving little room for improvement through the amortization of
Gaussian elimination. In the sublinear-weight regime, by contrast, the meet-in-
the-middle step need not be dominant. Our approach is therefore particularly
relevant in this setting.

5.1   Our MAGE-Stern Algorithm
In Reduce-and-Prange (Algorithm 3.1), the reduction performed at iteration i
relies on the assumption that the error vector e vanishes on a prescribed set of
bi coordinates. These coordinates can consequently be eliminated, producing a
smaller decoding instance.
    Stern’s algorithm follows a different strategy: it searches for an error vector
whose restriction to the information set has a prescribed nonzero weight. Con-
sequently, the reduction mechanism of Reduce-and-Prange cannot be applied
directly. Nevertheless, incremental guesses on the error support can still be com-
bined with partial Gaussian eliminations. This yields a new variant of Stern’s
algorithm based on Multilevel Amortized Gaussian Elimination, which we call
MAGE-Stern. Its pseudocode is given in Algorithm 5.1.

7     Projective MAGE-Stern
The security of many Pseudorandom Correlation Generator (PCG) protocols
relies on the hardness of either the classical decoding problem Decq (n, k, t) or
the regular decoding problem d-Decq (n, k, t) over large finite fields. In this sec-

such parameter regimes. Its main idea is to combine the Gaussian-elimination

explained at the end of Section 3.1, the latter reduces the enumeration cost of
the meet-in-the-middle step by a factor of approximately q by carrying out the
search in projective space. For very large q, this technique makes Stern’s algo-

Prange’s algorithm.

8     Application to Pseudorandom Correlation Generators

We now assess the security of PCG-based protocols by evaluating Projective
MAGE-Stern and its regular variant on the reference parameter sets proposed
in [10]. These protocols rely on the hardness of either the decoding problem
Decq (n, k, t) or its regular counterpart t-Decq (n, k, t).
    We compare our results with the best currently known attacks. In particular,
we consider the estimator of [46], introduced in [31], which incorporates classical
ISD algorithms [36,23,5], the dual attack of [16], and the algebraic and hybrid
attacks targeting the regular setting [11,43]. We additionally include the Reduce-
and-Prange algorithm of [30], which is not currently covered by this estimator.
